faq.q: Can I cancel a solar contract in Las Vegas?
faq.a: Possibly, but not automatically. In Las Vegas, whether you can cancel depends on the agreement, how and where it was signed or sold, whether installation has begun, and applicable Nevada law. Review the contract and preserve communications, recordings, invoices, and financing papers. Nevada’s Attorney General identifies solar-specific consumer protections and a rescission process, but the result depends on the facts and contract. faq.q: What should I gather before seeking cancellation?

A complaint may prompt agency review, but it does not itself cancel a contract or provide legal representation.

faq.q: What records should I gather for a solar contract review in Austin, Texas?
faq.a: Gather the signed agreement, loan or lease documents, disclosures, sales proposals, utility bills, installation records, and communications with the seller, installer, servicer, or lender.

faq.q: How long does a solar contract dispute take in Texas?
faq.a: Timing varies with the agreement, facts, parties involved, selected process, and applicable law. No result or timeline can be determined before an individual review.

faq.q: Where can I verify solar-company complaint information for Austin?
faq.a: Check current records from the Texas attorney general, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Trade Commission, and other official regulators. Third-party ratings and complaint totals can change.

faq.q: What is the TDU delivery fee and why am I still paying it with solar?
faq.a: In deregulated Texas markets, the Transmission and Distribution Utility (TDU) charges a delivery fee of $40-55/month that solar panels cannot eliminate. Many solar sales reps fail to disclose this charge, leading homeowners to believe their electric bill will be $0.

faq.q: Can I sue my solar lender (GoodLeap, Mosaic) directly?
faq.a: Under the FTC Holder Rule (16 CFR 433), you can assert claims against your lender for any violations committed by the solar dealer/installer. This includes TILA violations, misrepresentation, and fraud. The lender is liable up to the amount you have paid.
